newsitem.title: HAITI: Ousted dictator's voice heard again in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Ousted dictator's voice heard again in Haiti.

text.p: Ousted dictator Jean-Claude Duvalier was the talk of Haiti on Wednesday after several Haitian radio stations aired his voice for the first time since he was forced into exile 11 years ago.

In the four-minute broadcast on Radio Vision 2000 and other stations on Tuesday, Duvalier said he wanted to play a role in the country's transformation. The tape was made for Radio Toro Boeuf, a Miami Creole-language programme, and was believed to have been taped at Duvalier's home in France.
"It's been a long time since you've heard from me. It hurts me a lot to hear how things are going for you," he said.

Haiti's political scene has calmed since U.S.-led troops returned the first freely elected president, Jean-Bertrand Aristide, to power in 1994, ending a run of violent government transitions that began with Duvalier's ouster in 1986.

But the hemisphere's poorest nation remains gripped by crushing poverty and seemingly intractable social problems, leading some residents to look back warmly on the relative prosperity of the long dictatorship of Duvalier and his father, Francois.

Some supporters marched with black-and-red Duvalierist flags in the Haitian countryside in February when it was decided that a 10-year ban on Duvalierists running in elections would not end in time for their candidates to compete in parliamentary balloting on April 6.
Duvalier did not suggest in the broadcast that he planned to return to Haiti, where he would face arrest on charges he stole hundreds of millions of dollars from state coffers.
Supporters have said they were organising to bring Duvalier back to Haiti for the 2000 presidential election, when Aristide also is expected to be a candidate again.
Aristide was barred from seeking reelection in 1995 by a provision in the Haitian constitution that barred politicians from serving consecutive terms as president.
